title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
Imagine you are managing an investment fund. Your goal is simple: earn the highest possible return for your investors. However, you cannot invest however you like. Your fund has several rules: no single stock can account for more than 10% of the portfolio, and the maximum drawdown must remain below 30%. Maximum drawdown measures the largest cumulative decline in portfolio value from a previous peak to a subsequent low. It is one way of describing how much an investor could lose during a bad period.
There is another complication. In your estimates, investments with higher expected returns also tend to have greater downside risk. Putting everything into the investment with the highest expected return might therefore violate the fund’s risk limit.
This is a classic economic problem: how do we maximize an objective when some choices are not allowed? The method of Lagrange multipliers offers a systematic way to answer this question. It is useful not only in portfolio management but also in consumer choice, production planning, and resource allocation.

title: “Blog Post 1 for AEDS 6400” author: “Zhengyang Ding” output: html_document —
Suppose you are standing at the foot of a mountain, planning to climb to the top, and then return to the ground at the foot on the other side. Now imagine that there is a tunnel through the mountain, connecting your starting point and end point. Comparing the relative spatial location of the tunnel and your travel path with respect to the horizon, what do you find?
Through quick observation, you would discover that the tunnel lies completely beneath your travel route. In fact, you would realize that for any two points on or within the mountain, the straight line connecting them always lies inside the mountain. What does this phenomenon imply? What characteristics does the mountain’s landscape have?
The mountain, from a mathematical view, is a three-dimensional region. The property of this solid set that yields this phenomenon is convexity. A region is convex if the straight line segment connecting any two points within the region always lies inside the region. In two-dimensional space, a function is convex if its graph, within the range of any two points on it, lies below the straight line connecting the two points.
In mathematics, we define the convexity of a function as
\[
f\left(\lambda x_1 + (1-\lambda)x_2\right)
\leq
\lambda f(x_1) + (1-\lambda)f(x_2),
\qquad
\forall x_1,x_2\in\operatorname{dom}(f),\quad
\forall \lambda\in[0,1].
\]
There are several operations that preserve convexity, such as nonnegative weighted sums, composition with affine functions, and pointwise maximum. For example, if \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\) are convex functions and \(\alpha_i\geq0\), then the nonnegative weighted sum of the functions
\[
f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i f_i(x)
\]
is also convex.
To extend the use of convexity in solving mathematical problems, we expand the combination from two points to \(n\) points, then we get the definition of convex combination as follows:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i,
\qquad
\lambda_i\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i=1.
\]
This form of the weighted sum of variables with parameters reminds us of the definition of expectation. If the \(\lambda_i\)’s are interpreted as probabilities, then convex combinations could be interpreted by expected values. We therefore come to the following inequality named Jensen’s inequality:
\[
f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i\right)
\leq
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i f(x_i),
\]
or equivalently,
\[
f\left(\mathbb{E}[X]\right)
\leq
\mathbb{E}[f(X)].
\]
Following the definition of convex functions, we may also derive the convexity of sets. A set \(C\) is convex if, for any two points \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) in \(C\),
\[
\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\in C,
\qquad
\forall\lambda\in[0,1].
\]
Moreover, the sublevel set of a convex function is also a convex set. For a convex function \(f\), its sublevel set at level \(\alpha\) is defined as
\[
C_{\alpha}
=
\left\{
x\in\operatorname{dom}(f)
\mid
f(x)\leq\alpha
\right\}.
\]
The convexity of feasible sets is particularly useful when we attempt to solve optimization problems (a feasible set for a series of constraints is the set of every point that satisfies all the constraints). When the feasible set is convex, together with appropriate properties with respect to the objective function, optimization problems often allow us to employ simplified calculation approaches and produce interior solutions.
Why should economists care about convexity and its connection with optimization? Convex preferences, feasible sets, and objective functions are closely related to whether optimization problems have well-behaved solutions and why local information could sometimes imply information on the global problem.

title: Are Ratings of Films Within Top Lists Still Valuable?
text:
Douban, a popular film and book review website from China, has a good reputation and a huge amount of audience who carefully rate and comment on films and books from different countries and times. It is particularly known for its top 250 film list, which is ranked among all the films in the world. The list is considered a useful tool for those who want to watch a film with good reputations. As a film fan, I have frequently referred to this list, along with specific comments and ratings, when selecting classic films to watch.



The Webpage of Douban’s Top 250 Film List


The ranking of the list is carefully calculated through algorithms, according to the weighted sum of effective ratings from reliable reviewers. This is realized through the analysis of the overall behavior of each reviewer, which the platform could monitor. This brings a high reliability for the list, while the specific calculation remain different. Plus, the audience would not blindly follow the list when selecting films, as they have specific tastes for different types of films. Thus, they would still check the basic info of a film like I do, while the list offers a general spectrum.
The most direct way to refer to a film’s quality is the average rating for each film, which is visible to the audience. However, as this is already a list of top films, the ratings as references could imposes questions: are they still valuable when the fluctuation is highly restricted for the top list? Particularly, as commenters may be more careful and picky when giving high rates, could there be any bias for the Chinese view films of different types?

title: Are Ratings of Films Within Top Lists Still Valuable?
text:
Douban, a popular film and book review website from China, has a good reputation and a huge amount of audience who carefully rate and comment on films and books from different countries and times. It is particularly known for its top 250 film list, which is ranked among all the films in the world. The list is considered a useful tool for those who want to watch a film with good reputations. As a film fan, I have frequently referred to this list, along with specific comments and ratings, when selecting classic films to watch.



The Webpage of Douban’s Top 250 Film List


The ranking of the list is carefully calculated through algorithms, according to the weighted sum of effective ratings from reliable reviewers. This is realized through the analysis of the overall behavior of each reviewer, which the platform could monitor. This brings a high reliability for the list, while the specific calculation remain different. Plus, the audience would not blindly follow the list when selecting films, as they have specific tastes for different types of films. Thus, they would still check the basic info of a film like I do, while the list offers a general spectrum.
The most direct way to refer to a film’s quality is the average rating for each film, which is visible to the audience. However, as this is already a list of top films, the ratings as references could imposes questions: are they still valuable when the fluctuation is highly restricted for the top list? Particularly, as commenters may be more careful and picky when giving high rates, could there be any bias for the Chinese view films of different types?

title: Are Ratings of Films Within Top Lists Still Valuable?
text:
Data Analysis
In this blog, we employ RVEST using R to scrape data on the top 250 film list from the Douban website, attempting to answer these questions through some simple data analysis. We collect data on the ranking, country, year, and genre of each film within the Top 250 list, and again, employ R to conduct analysis and visualization.We group films respectively according to the ranking (50 films a group), production year (a decade for each group),the genre, and the country (we only analyze the major countries here). We then calculate and plot the average rating for each group.
We first discover that the average rating does not necessarily correlate with the ranking of a film. Indeed, we do not observe a downward trend of average ratings along with rankings (the invisible effective ratings follow this rule, as they are exactly the reference of the ranking!). Therefore, we may tell that the visible average ratings plays an insignificant part within this top list, as the effective rating is hardly correlated with the visible rating.



Average Rating by Ranking Group


We then check if different categories of films would exhibit different ratings. Different categories are not supposed to be assigned with different art values, therefore this might indicate some preferences of Chinese audience.
Regarding genre, we find that fantasy and mystery films receive particularly low scores, and crime films receive lower scores to some degree as well. It could be speculated that these are relatively niche genres, which possess relatively fewer audiences with strong preferences. Other genres generally receive high scores, with documentaries receiving the highest rating.



Average Rating by Genre Group


Moving to the category of country, because countries of production are relatively centralized for top films, we select some major countries for comparison, including China Hongkong, China Macao, China Taiwan, France, Britain, the U.S., Japan and South Korea. We find that Chinese audience seems to be critical on home country films compared with western major countries. A special finding is that Japan receives particularly low ratings, while South Korean films are highly recognized. This may also be explained by subjective tastes.



Average Rating by Country


Another attempt we made is to group years of production and see if there are any regularities. We find steady fluctuations by decades, without a strong direction of trend.



Average Rating by year

title: Are Ratings of Films Within Top Lists Still Valuable?
text:
Conclusion
In general, through the data we scraped from Douban’s top film list, we managed to conduct a series of statistical analysis. We find that the visible ratings among the top-listed films are of insignificant reference value, as they remain stable across rankings of the list. We also find that the Chinese audience might has preferences over documentaries and South Korean films, while domestic films, Japanese films, and films under the genre of mystery or fantasy receive generally less preferences.
The findings help us rationally and carefully treat the ratings on major review platforms. Our findings imply that visible ratings from the well-known Douban platform might lose effectiveness within the top 250 list, and ratings on films of certain types (Fantasy, Japanese, domestic, etc.) could be biased when cross-compared with other categories. It is possible that similar patterns exist among other similar rating platforms, which might be a path for future investigations.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Educational background of labor is an important determinant of labor market outcomes. People with higher levels of education could enjoy better employment opportunities and higher salaries, while they may also experience less unemployment. Meanwhile, the relationship between education and the labor market varies across time, as different macroeconomic backgrounds, market structure, and other external factors could all help shape this relationship.
This blog post explores the following question: how are education attainment and labor market outcomes related in the United States, and how does this relationship change over time?
This analysis targets adults in the U.S., aged 25-64, and the observation covers the period of 2000-2024. Individuals are divided into five groups according to educational attainment: less than high school, high school diploma, some college or an associate degree, four years of college or a bachelor’s degree, and five or more years of college or a graduate degree.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Educational background of labor is an important determinant of labor market outcomes. People with higher levels of education could enjoy better employment opportunities and higher salaries, while they may also experience less unemployment. Meanwhile, the relationship between education and the labor market varies across time, as different macroeconomic backgrounds, market structure, and other external factors could all help shape this relationship.
This blog post explores the following question: how are education attainment and labor market outcomes related in the United States, and how does this relationship change over time?
This analysis targets adults in the U.S., aged 25-64, and the observation covers the period of 2000-2024. Individuals are divided into five groups according to educational attainment: less than high school, high school diploma, some college or an associate degree, four years of college or a bachelor’s degree, and five or more years of college or a graduate degree.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Data and Mechanism
I employ the following three dimensions to evaluate labor market outcomes: whether individuals worked during the year, how much their income was (if they worked), and whether they experienced unemployment during the year. These dimensions respectively evaluate access, return, and risk regarding employment.
The data source is the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey (CPS). The CPS is a nationally representative survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the ASEC covers information on work, income, and other socioeconomic elements.
I use individual samples during the period 2001-2025 because surveys collected information from the previous year instead of the current year. Therefore, the observation window corresponds to 2000-2024 as expected.
The main explanatory variable, educational attainment, is measured using the EDUC variable. EDUC records the highest level of schooling or degree completed, therefore covering many grades and degrees. They are categorized into five groups: less than high school, high school diploma, some college or associate degree, four years of college or bachelor’s degree, and five or more years of college or a graduate degree. This is the reference group for surveyed individuals in the analysis.
For the first dimension, we calculate the share of people who worked during the year among the sum for each group. This comes from the variable WORKLY from the CPS dataset. The same is conducted for the third dimension, where we calculate the share of individuals who experienced unemployment during the year. This comes from the variable WKSUNEM1. For convenience, we will refer to these two dimensions as employment rate and unemployment in the analysis of the results, while one should not that our calculation may differ from the usual approaches in defining employment and unemployment rates.
For the second dimension, we use the variable INCWAGE as the original data source, which reports income in nominal U.S. dollars. We first transfer the income to real terms using the 2024 CPI as the basis (The CPI data comes from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis FRED), then calculate the median for each group. We select the median instead of the mean value due to the highly skewed distribution of data.
All the shares and descriptive values above are calculated in the weighted form according to the person-level sampling weight from the dataset. This enables our findings to depict the whole U.S. labor market.
This produces three consistent time-series visualizations that can be compared directly across education groups.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Findings



Employment Experience Share by Educational Attainment


For the first dimension on the relation between education attainment and employment rate, we can tell from the figure that the higher the education level is, the higher the employment rate will be. This pattern is consistent over time, with individuals with 5+ years of college having an employment rate of around 90%, and individuals with less-than-high-school education having an employment rate fluctuating between 60% and 65%. From the time series visualization, we can also observe that the magnitude of fluctuation is negatively correlated with education level. Groups with higher education levels experience slight fluctuations in the employment rate over time. For instance, the downward slope of the employment rate is the steepest for the group with less-than-high-school education during the 2008 financial crisis.



Median Annual Wage by Educational Attainment


For the dimension of income level, we also observe a consistent pattern that individuals with higher education levels would receive higher income. The group with the highest education level has a median income that is around 300% of the income level of the group with the lowest education level.



Unemployment Experience Share by Educational Attainment


For the dimension of unemployment existence, we also observe that individuals with better education are less likely to become unemployed. This time-consistent regularity complements the first dimension of our evaluation, implying lower risks of unemployment. The difference in fluctuation magnitude is not observed across different groups of individuals.

title: How are Educational Attainment and Labor Market Outcomes Related in the U.S.?
text:
Conclusion
In general, our three sets of visual analyses reveal a consistent relationship between educational attainment and labor market outcomes in the United States from 2000 to 2024. Individuals with higher levels of education have a higher chance of working during the year, receive higher median wages, and are less likely to experience unemployment. These general trends persist over the observation window, and less-educated groups tend to experience larger fluctuations in employment. One should note that these findings are descriptive rather than causal, as other elements, such as work experience, occupation, and industry, may also contribute to the observed differences.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Buying a home today feels impossible for many Americans. But is this purely because houses are getting too expensive? Not necessarily. A booming housing market might be offset by rising incomes, and high price tags can sometimes be swallowed if borrowing costs are historically low.
This blog answers the following question: How has housing affordability in the United States changed over time, and what roles have house prices, mortgage rates, and household income played in this change?

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Buying a home today feels impossible for many Americans. But is this purely because houses are getting too expensive? Not necessarily. A booming housing market might be offset by rising incomes, and high price tags can sometimes be swallowed if borrowing costs are historically low.
This blog answers the following question: How has housing affordability in the United States changed over time, and what roles have house prices, mortgage rates, and household income played in this change?

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Data
The data source for this blog is the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis FRED database. We use its API to scrape data from the website.
Four FRED series are used:









Variable
FRED Series
Original Frequency
Role




Median sales price of new houses
MSPUS
Quarterly
Housing price


30-year fixed mortgage rate
MORTGAGE30US
Weekly
Borrowing cost


Real median household income
MEHOINUSA672N
Annual
Household purchasing power


Consumer Price Index
CPIAUCSL
Monthly
Inflation adjustment



The original data of different variables involve different frequencies, thus for the consistency within our analysis, the weekly mortgage rate and monthly CPI are transformed into quarterly averages. The quarterly median house price is kept at its original frequency. Annual median household income is matched to each quarter within the corresponding year.
For monetary values, the nominal median house price is converted into the real value to 2025 dollars using the CPI:
\[
RealHousePrice_t =
NominalHousePrice_t
\times
\frac{CPI_{2025}}{CPI_t}
\]
This adjustment allows house prices from different periods to be compared according to the same purchasing power.
Finally, I construct the house-price-to-income ratio:
\[
PriceIncomeRatio_t =
\frac{RealHousePrice_t}
{RealMedianHouseholdIncome_t}
\]
A higher value indicates that the price of ordinary houses is high relative to household’s average income, implying the average level of housing affordability.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Visualization Strategy
I use three time-series visualizations to analyze the trend on housing affordability. Each visualization focuses on a different component of housing affordability, and together they provide a broader picture of how the housing market has changed.



Figure 1: House Price Trend


The first visualization plots the median sales price of new houses in constant 2025 U.S. dollars. Looking at the real house prices, there is a long-run upward trend in general. Despite a few temporary downturns that might be correlated with macro economic recessions (like the 2008 financial crisis), the general trend goes up, and the level of real house prices is considerably higher in the 2020s than it was during the 1960s. The price approximately doubled over the past 60 years.



Figure 2: Mortgage Rate Trend


The house price alone doesn’t tell the whole story. The second visualization plots the quarterly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate. Mortgage rates represent the cost of financing a home purchase. At a same house price, a higher mortgage rate lowers the affordability.
The figure shows that the 30-year mortgage rate grew to approximately 18% in 1963-1980, then gradually declined for decades until 2020. The decline became particularly pronounced during the COVID-19 period, when mortgage rates reached a level of around 3%. After 2021, mortgage rates recovered significantly from the bottom level to around 7%.
This pattern implies that housing price alone cannot fully describe housing affordability during some period of times. During 1980-2020, the lowered cost of financing accompanied the rising real house price, keeping house affordability somewhat affordable. By contrast, the high house price in the 2020s combined an increase in mortgage rate created a worsened affordability environment.



Figure 3: Price-to-Income Ratio


The third visualization plots the ratio of real median house prices to real median household income, which directly compares the cost of housing with household income. Intense fluctuations are observed, with the cycle’s peak increasing each time.
The ratio was relatively stable around 4 in the mid-1980s and early 1990s. It then increased during the late 1990s and early 2000s, reaching 5 before the housing market crisis.
The ratio declined significantly when the financial crisis came in the late 2000s, which is consistent with the sharp decline in house prices shown in Figure 1.
After the financial crisis, the ratio recovered. During the 2010s, housing prices grew faster than household income, pushing the ratio upward, and then a setback came again in the late 2010s. The increase went sharp during 2020–2023, when the ratio approached 6.
The post-pandemic decline after 2022 is also clearly illustrated from the graph. The ratio falls substantially from its peak as real house prices declined. However, our graph 2 complements the explanation of regularity here, as mortgage rates increased substantially during the same period, which means that the cost of financing a home became considerably higher even though the price-to-income ratio declined. This comparison between Figures 2 and 3 indicates that the price-to-income ratio and mortgage rates capture different dimensions of affordability, which are both significant.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Conclusion
This project analyzes how housing affordability in the United States has changed over time by combining three dimensions of the housing market: real house prices, mortgage rates, and the house-price-to-income ratio.
The analysis shows that real house prices have increased significantly in the long run, despite several major downturns. At the same time, mortgage rates have experienced a long-term decline from the exceptionally high levels of the early 1980s, followed by a sharp increase after 2021.
The house-price-to-income ratio offers a trend of the relationship between housing costs and household resources. Its increase during the 2000s and especially the early 2020s suggests that housing became increasingly expensive relative to household income. The previous analysis on mortgage rate could help with the explanation to this trend.
The general takeaway of this study is that housing affordability relies on the interaction between housing price, household income, and borrowing cost. Taking early 2020s as an instance, the rapid house-price growth increased the price of housing relative to household income, while historically low mortgage rates temporarily reduced financing costs. After 2021, however, rising mortgage rates added another source of financial pressure for potential home buyers.
The visualization suggests that the economic burden of purchasing a house has increased over the long run, while this burden may have changed through different channels. Looking at house prices, income, and mortgage rates together offers a more informative picture of housing affordability than focusing on any single indicator.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Data and Method
To investigate this, I used historical data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED) through API access. I looked at three key variables: the median sales price of new houses, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, and the real median household income.
The observation window is 1963-2024, and variables are recorded on a seasonal basis (income data was coded only since 1980s). To ensure an apples-to-apples comparison over decades, I adjusted nominal house prices and incomes for inflation using the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
The analysis is conducted with three figures. The first and second firueres respectively use the variables of real housing price and 30-year mortgage rate. For the third graph, I calculate a price-to-income ratio that directly compares the cost of an average house to the average household’s purchasing power.

title: Housing Affordability in the United States: Prices, Mortgage Rates, and Household Income
text:
Takeaway
Method: I used Census FRED API data to analyze three core components of housing: inflation-adjusted house prices, 30-year mortgage rates, and the price-to-income ratio. They together offer an overview of the general housing affordability in the U.S. over the past decades.
Wage-Price Disconnect: Real house prices have surged over the long run, significantly outpacing household income growth and pushing the price-to-income ratio to historic highs.
The Rate Illusion: Historically low mortgage rates countered the severity of rising house prices in 1980-2020, temporarily keeping monthly payments somewhat affordable.
The Double Squeeze: The recent post-pandemic (after 2020) spike in mortgage rates, combined with already high housing prices, has fundamentally elevated the economic burden for potential home buyers.
Core Insight: Housing affordability is not just about the price tag; it relies heavily on the interaction between prices, income, and borrowing costs. Looking at any single indicator fails to capture the true financial burden on American households.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Is the American Dream geographically concentrated? As the national debate around inequality deepens, we explore the geographical distribution of people at different income levels. We look beyond national averages and zoom into the county level, which is the building blocks of local economies.
In this blog, we attempt to answer the following question: What is the geographical distribution of high- and low-income counties in the U.S., and is this spatial characteristic changing over time?

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Is the American Dream geographically concentrated? As the national debate around inequality deepens, we explore the geographical distribution of people at different income levels. We look beyond national averages and zoom into the county level, which is the building blocks of local economies.
In this blog, we attempt to answer the following question: What is the geographical distribution of high- and low-income counties in the U.S., and is this spatial characteristic changing over time?

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Data and Method
To conduct this analysis, we extract data county-level median household income from the U.S. Census Bureau through API, drawing on the American Community Survey (ACS). Because single-year ACS estimates only cover heavily populated areas, we used ACS 5-year estimates to ensure complete, reliable geographic coverage across the entire country. The latest round of statistics come from 2024, and we also extract statistics from a decade ago (2014) for comparative analysis.
Using R, we merge median household income data with geographic boundary shapefiles at the county level. To untangle genuine spatial shifts from the effects of inflation, we calculate each county’s relative income rank by assigning them to quintiles from the lowest 20% to the highest 20% nationally. In this way, we get to map the distributions of relative county-level income to the spatial map.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Analytical Findings
The Current Landscape: 2024



Figure 1: 2024 Relvative Income Distribution


The relative county-level income distribution map for 2024 reveals a clear geographic polarization. High-income counties (the top 20%) are not scattered randomly; they are tightly clustered along the Northeast Corridor, the West Coast tech hubs (like the Bay Area and Seattle), and a handful of booming inland metros (e.g., Denver, Austin, Nashville). Conversely, the lowest-income counties (bottom 20%) form a massive, contiguous block across the American South, stretching from the Appalachian Mountains down through the Mississippi Delta, alongside pockets of the Southwest.



Figure 2: 2024 Absolute Income Distribution


To validate this, the absolute median household income map (our median income data is directly used to map this) corroborates our findings. The spatial patterns align perfectly: the darkest, wealthiest counties (often exceeding 150,000 in median income) correspond to the coastal pink clusters, while the lowest brackets (frequently below 50,000) mirror the Southern red belt. This tells us that the relative ranking does reflect real wealth gaps between regions.
A Decade of Change: 2014 vs. 2024



Figure 3: 2014 Relvative Income Distribution


When we compare 2024 to a decade ago (2014), the general revelation is the stickiness of spatial inequality. The economic landscape of the wealthy coasts and the impoverished South remain remarkably unchanged.
Under the general revelation, a closer look reveals a hardening Matthew Effect (the rich get richer). Over the decade, certain suburban and exurban counties adjacent to major metropolitan hubs have shifted from middle-tier to top-tier categories. Meanwhile, many rural counties in the Midwest and South that were previously middle-income have slipped down the rankings. The map shows a subtle but significant consolidation of high-income status into fewer, more concentrated metro areas, while the areas left behind are sprawling.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Takeaway
Method: We extract Census ACS 5-year estimates and use R to map county-level relative income quintiles across the U.S. for both 2014 and 2024.
Spatial Polarization: The map reveals severe geographic clustering, with high-income counties concentrated on the coasts and low-income counties forming a massive, contiguous block across the South region.
Structural Stickiness: A decade-over-decade comparison shows strong persistence, as the broad geographic contours of wealth and poverty remain mainly unchanged.
Metropolitan Concentration: Over time, an emerging “Matthew Effect” is visible, with wealth further concentrating into core metropolitan hubs, while many rural counties slip down the relative rankings.
Core Insight: American income inequality fundamentally has spatial regularities, as economic opportunity and mobility remain tied to one’s zip code.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
text:
Analytical Findings - The Current Landscape: 2024



Figure 1: 2024 Relvative Income Distribution


The relative county-level income distribution map for 2024 reveals a clear geographic polarization. High-income counties (the top 20%) are not scattered randomly; they are tightly clustered along the Northeast Corridor, the West Coast tech hubs (like the Bay Area and Seattle), and a handful of booming inland metros (e.g., Denver, Austin, Nashville). Conversely, the lowest-income counties (bottom 20%) form a massive, contiguous block across the American South, stretching from the Appalachian Mountains down through the Mississippi Delta, alongside pockets of the Southwest.



Figure 2: 2024 Absolute Income Distribution


To validate this, the absolute median household income map (our median income data is directly used to map this) corroborates our findings. The spatial patterns align perfectly: the darkest, wealthiest counties (often exceeding 150,000 in median income) correspond to the coastal pink clusters, while the lowest brackets (frequently below 50,000) mirror the Southern red belt. This tells us that the relative ranking does reflect real wealth gaps between regions.

title: The Geography of U.S. Income Distribution: A Decade of Sticky Divides
section: Analytical Findings - A Decade of Change: 2014 versus 2024
text:
Analytical Findings - A Decade of Change: 2014 versus 2024



Figure 3: 2014 Relvative Income Distribution


When we compare 2024 to a decade ago (2014), the general revelation is the stickiness of spatial inequality. The economic landscape of the wealthy coasts and the impoverished South remain remarkably unchanged.
Under the general revelation, a closer look reveals a hardening Matthew Effect (the rich get richer). Over the decade, certain suburban and exurban counties adjacent to major metropolitan hubs have shifted from middle-tier to top-tier categories. Meanwhile, many rural counties in the Midwest and South that were previously middle-income have slipped down the rankings. The map shows a subtle but significant consolidation of high-income status into fewer, more concentrated metro areas, while the areas left behind are sprawling.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Introduction
Inter-generational mobility research requires us to connect information about parents and children. In longitudinal data, parent-child relationships and income information are often stored separately, making data matching an important part of the empirical workflow.
This tutorial shows how SQL within Python can be used to match parents and children in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID). The main goal is to demonstrate how four basic SQL operations—SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, and aggregation—turn separate longitudinal records into a usable parent-child dataset.
After constructing the matched sample, I use family total income to estimate inter-generational income elasticity (IGE). I then compare income measured in one year with income averaged over two years to illustrate why a single income observation may be a noisy measure of long-run economic status.


Data and the Matching Problem
The data come from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID). The analysis uses individual identifiers, family identifiers, parent-identification variables, age, and total family income.
For this tutorial, “income” means total income of the family unit in which a person is observed, rather than individual labor earnings. Thus, child income is the income of the child’s family, while parent income is the income of the family in which the matched parent is observed.
The analysis uses income from 2022 for the single-year comparison and income from 2020 and 2022 for the multi-year comparison. The working-age sample is restricted to individuals aged 25–64 in 2022.
The matching problem is simple:

Given a child, how can we identify the child’s parent and then retrieve the family income of both the child and the parent?

The PSID parent-identification file provides the relationship between children and their biological parents. We construct a permanent person identifier from the interview number and person number:

Child ID = PID2 + PID3
Mother ID = PID4 + PID5
Father ID = PID23 + PID24

The same person-ID construction is used in the individual longitudinal data, allowing the parent-identification data to be connected to the income data.
The distinction between person identifiers and family identifiers is important. The person identifier tells us who the individual is, while the family identifier tells us which family the individual belongs to in a particular year. We first use the person identifier to establish the parent-child relationship and then use the family identifier to retrieve family income.


SQL Workflow
The matching task is fundamentally a relational-data problem.
The workflow is:
Parent Identification File
↓
Child ID + Parent ID
↓ JOIN
Individual Longitudinal Data
↓
Family Income by Year
↓ GROUP BY + aggregation
Matched Parent-Child Dataset
SQL is useful because one table describes family relationships while another contains person-year observations. SQL allows these tables to be connected through identifiers and summarized systematically.
I use SQL within Python through SQLite. This keeps the matching process reproducible while making the relational operations explicit. The implementation is divided into three stages when coding, including data process, data match, and data analysis. Check the GitHub repository for the complete code for each part of them. Below introduces the key sections of the workflow with an emphasis on the use of SQLite in Python.


Loading the Data into SQLite
The cleaned individual data contain the variables needed for the income analysis, including:

person_id
family_id
family_income
year
age

The parent-identification data contain the variables needed to construct the child, mother, and father IDs.
These datasets are loaded into a SQLite database as separate tables. The parent-identification table describes who is related to whom, while the individual table describes where each person is observed and what family income is associated with that observation.
The two tables can then be connected using their common person identifiers.


Constructing the Parent-Child Relationship
The first step is to construct permanent IDs for the child, mother, and father from the PSID identification variables.
The resulting relationship information can be represented conceptually as:



child_id
parent_id

5_1



Each child can therefore be connected to one or two parents.
The parent-child relationship table serves as a bridge table. It does not contain the income measures yet. Its purpose is to identify which parent records should be connected to each child.
The next step is to use these IDs to retrieve the corresponding parent and child records from the longitudinal individual data.


SQL Operation 1: SELECT
SELECT determines which variables are returned from the database.
For this application, the relevant variables include child ID, parent ID, family income, family ID, age, and year.
For example, after the parent-child relationship has been established, SELECT tells SQL to return the child ID together with the relevant parent and child income measures.
The key point is that SELECT determines what information we want to retrieve. It does not itself perform the parent-child match.


SQL Operation 2: JOIN
JOIN performs the actual matching.
The parent-child bridge table contains parent_id and child_id, while the individual table contains person_id. The two tables are connected by matching these identifiers.
Conceptually:
parent_id → person_id → parent’s family record
and
child_id → person_id → child’s family record
The same individual table is therefore used twice: once to retrieve the parent record and once to retrieve the child record.
For the single-year analysis, the matching is performed using the 2022 observations.
We also exclude cases where the parent and child are observed in the same family. This prevents their family-level income measures from being mechanically identical.
The key role of JOIN in this project is therefore:

Use individual identifiers to connect the parent-child relationship to the appropriate longitudinal records.



SQL Operation 3: GROUP BY
After the JOIN, a child with two observed parents can appear in multiple records.
For example:



child_id
parent_id
parent income

60,000


4_3
4_1
80,000



The final analysis requires one parental-income measure for each child.
GROUP BY organizes observations belonging to the same child into one group. In this application, the data are grouped at the child level so that information from multiple parents can be combined.
Thus:

GROUP BY changes the matched parent records into child-level groups that can then be summarized.



SQL Operation 4: Aggregation
After grouping the parent records, we use aggregation to construct the parental-income measure.
The main aggregation function is AVG().
If both parents are observed, their family incomes are averaged. For example, if the two parents have family incomes of $60,000 and $80,000:
[ ParentIncome = = 70,000. ]
If only one parent can be matched, the available parent’s family income is used.
Aggregation is also used across years when constructing the multi-year income measure.
The four SQL operations therefore have distinct roles:



SQL operation
Role in this application




SELECT
Choose the variables returned by the query


JOIN
Match parent/child IDs to individual records


GROUP BY
Organize records at the child level


AVG()
Aggregate information across parents or years



This is the core SQL workflow of the project:
Identifiers establish the relationship → JOIN retrieves the records → GROUP BY organizes multiple parents → aggregation constructs the final income measure.


Constructing Multi-Year Income
To compare single-year and multi-year measures, the same matching procedure is applied to both 2020 and 2022.
For each matched parent and child, we retrieve family income in both years.
The multi-year measures are then constructed as:
[ ParentIncome_{avg} = ]
and
[ ChildIncome_{avg} = . ]
This gives us two measures of economic status:

Single-year income: 2022 income.
Multi-year income: average income over 2020 and 2022.

The final sample is restricted to individuals aged 25–64 in 2022 and to observations with positive income.


Estimating the IGE
The intergenerational income elasticity (IGE) is estimated using:
[ (ChildIncome_i) = + (ParentIncome_i) + _i. ]
The coefficient () is the IGE. It measures the persistence of economic status across generations.
A larger IGE indicates a stronger association between parental and child income.
Two specifications are estimated:

Single-year IGE: using 2022 income.
Multi-year IGE: using average income from 2020 and 2022.

Both specifications use the same final matched sample, allowing the comparison to focus on the way income is measured.


Results
The final matched sample contains 1,635 observations.

The IGE increases from 0.245 when income is measured only in 2022 to 0.280 when income is averaged over 2020 and 2022.
The (R^2) also increases from 0.065 to 0.092. Since both models use the same 1,635 observations, the difference is not driven by a change in sample size.


Life-Cycle Bias and Long-Run Economic Status
A key problem with single-year income is that income varies over the life cycle.
For example, income may be relatively low early in a career, higher during peak working years, and lower again later in life. Therefore, income observed in one particular year may reflect both long-run economic status and the person’s position in the income life cycle.
Single-year income can also contain temporary shocks such as unemployment or unusually high earnings.
Conceptually:
[ Observed Income = Longrun Status + Lifecycle Component + Temporary Shock. ]
When one year’s income is used in the IGE regression, these components introduce noise into the measure of economic status.
Averaging income over several years can reduce the influence of temporary fluctuations. The resulting measure is more likely to capture persistent economic resources rather than a temporary income realization.
This matters because the purpose of IGE estimation is to measure economic persistence across generations, not simply the relationship between two particular income observations.
In this application, the IGE increases from 0.245 to 0.280 when income is averaged over 2020 and 2022. This pattern is consistent with the idea that multi-year income provides a more stable measure of long-run economic status.
This comparison does not prove that the two-year estimate is unbiased. Rather, it demonstrates why researchers often use multi-year income measures when studying long-run intergenerational mobility.


Key Takeaways
This tutorial demonstrates how SQL within Python can be used to construct a parent-child match from longitudinal PSID data.
The demo uses PSID longitudinal data to study intergenerational economic mobility by matching parents and children and comparing their family-level income.

SQL simplifies parent-child matching by using SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, and aggregation to connect individuals across longitudinal records.
Individual and family identifiers serve different purposes: individual IDs identify parents and children, while family IDs allow us to retrieve their family-level income.
JOIN connects records across people and years, while GROUP BY and aggregation summarize parent information at the child level.
SQL makes the matching process transparent and reproducible, providing a structured alternative to manual data manipulation.
The demo also shows why income measurement matters for IGE estimation. Using 2022 income gives an IGE of 0.245, compared with 0.280 when income is averaged over 2020–2022.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
Imagine you are managing an investment fund. Your goal is simple: earn the highest possible return for your investors. However, you cannot invest however you like. Your fund has several rules: no single stock can account for more than 10% of the portfolio, and the maximum drawdown must remain below 30%. Maximum drawdown measures the largest cumulative decline in portfolio value from a previous peak to a subsequent low. It is one way of describing how much an investor could lose during a bad period.
There is another complication. In your estimates, investments with higher expected returns also tend to have greater downside risk. Putting everything into the investment with the highest expected return might therefore violate the fund’s risk limit.
This is a classic economic problem: how do we maximize an objective when some choices are not allowed? The method of Lagrange multipliers offers a systematic way to answer this question. It is useful not only in portfolio management but also in consumer choice, production planning, and resource allocation.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
Turning the Problem into Mathematics
To understand the basic idea, let us simplify the fund’s investment choices into two categories. The first is a diversified equity portfolio, with an expected annual return of 12%. The second is a lower-risk asset portfolio, with an expected annual return of 4%. Let \(x\) and \(y\) represent the proportions invested in each category.
Because the fund must invest all its money,
\[
x+y=1.
\]
Its expected annual return, measured in percentage points, is
\[
R(x,y)=12x+4y.
\]
We also impose a simplified risk constraint:
\[
D(x)=8+44x\leq 30.
\]
Here, \(D(x)\) is an illustrative stress-risk score, expressed in percentage points. Its coefficients are hypothetical and are chosen only to demonstrate the method; it is not a forecast of actual maximum drawdown. The constraint implies that \(x\leq 0.5\).
Without a risk limit, the fund would put all its money into equities because their expected return is higher. With the limit, however, the most it can allocate to equities is 50%. The best feasible allocation is therefore \(x=0.5\) and \(y=0.5\), producing an expected return of 8%.
But how can we find this solution systematically, especially when there are many assets and constraints? This is where Lagrange multipliers become useful.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
The Logic of the Lagrangian
Instead of treating the objective and constraints as entirely separate problems, we combine them into one function:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}(x,y,\lambda,\mu)
={}&12x+4y\\
&+\lambda(1-x-y)\\
&+\mu\left[30-(8+44x)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term represents the return we want to maximize. The second incorporates the requirement that the entire portfolio be allocated. The third incorporates the risk limit. The new variables \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), called Lagrange multipliers, allow the optimization conditions to account for these restrictions.
The basic procedure is to find the point where the partial derivatives with respect to the decision variables are zero, while ensuring that the constraints are satisfied. For this example, the first-order conditions include
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y}=4-\lambda=0
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=12-\lambda-44\mu=0.
\]
These imply \(\lambda=4\) and \(\mu=8/44\approx 0.182\). Because the risk limit binds at the optimum, \(8+44x=30\), giving \(x=0.5\) and \(y=0.5\).
The important insight is that the multipliers are not arbitrary penalties selected by the fund manager. They are determined by the optimization conditions. In more general problems with inequality constraints, complementary slackness helps determine whether each constraint actually binds.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
section: What Does the Multiplier Tell Us?
text:
What Does the Multiplier Tell Us?
The multiplier \(\mu\) is the shadow price of the risk constraint. It measures how much the maximum expected return changes when the risk limit is relaxed by one unit, near the optimum.
Here, \(\mu=8/44\approx 0.182\). Raising the risk-score ceiling from 30 to 31 allows a larger equity allocation, increasing the model’s maximum expected annual return from 8.00% to about 8.18%. The multiplier therefore puts a number on the trade-off between accepting more risk and earning a higher return. This is a local result from our simplified model, not a guarantee about real investment performance.
In more complex problems, inequality constraints are handled using the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, which also identify whether a constraint is binding at the optimum.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
The Takeaway
Lagrange multipliers do more than provide a mathematical trick for solving constrained optimization problems. They offer a way to balance competing objectives while respecting real limitations. The central lesson is that the best decision is not necessarily the one with the highest possible return in isolation. It is the best decision among those that are feasible—and the multipliers help explain how much the constraints matter.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
References and Data Note
No empirical dataset is used in this example. All portfolio returns, risk-score coefficients, and investment constraints are illustrative assumptions.

Investor.gov: Introduction to Investing — background on asset allocation and diversification.
Goldberg and Mahmoud (2014), Drawdown: From Practice to Theory and Back Again — background on drawdown as a measure of investment risk.
Khan Academy: Interpretation of Lagrange Multipliers — the shadow-price interpretation.

title: Lagrange Multipliers: Making the Best Decision Under Constraints
text:
Takeaways

Set the objective and constraints. Define what you want to maximize or minimize, then specify the limits that feasible choices must satisfy.
Build the Lagrangian. Combine the objective function and constraints using Lagrange multipliers, then use the first-order conditions and the constraints to find the optimum.
Interpret the multipliers. A multiplier on a binding constraint measures the marginal value of relaxing that constraint—the change in the best achievable objective from a small relaxation.
Use the result to make decisions. Multipliers show which constraints are costly and help evaluate whether relaxing a limit could improve the outcome.
